lessons.title: Watching animals and reporting what you see
lessons.html:
Know what normal looks like

You see the animals every day. You are often the first person to notice when something is wrong. To see a problem, you must first know what a healthy animal looks like.

A healthy animal

  • Is alert. It looks up when you come near.
  • Stays with the herd or flock.
  • Eats and drinks well. Cattle and sheep chew the cud when they rest.
  • Walks easily on all four legs.
  • Has bright eyes and a clean nose.
  • Has a shiny coat or clean wool.
  • Breathes slowly and quietly when resting.
  • Has normal dung. Not too runny, not too hard.

Physical attributes to look at

Look at each animal's size, body condition (fat or thin), coat, eyes, nose, mouth, legs, feet, udder and tail end. Look at its ear tag or brand so you know which animal it is.

How to watch

  1. Watch the group from a distance first. Animals act normally when they are calm.
  2. Then walk slowly through the camp or kraal.
  3. Look at every animal from both sides.
  4. Watch them move.

Record and report

Write down what you see in the notebook or on the record sheet. Write the animal's number, the date, and what you saw. For example: Cow 214, 3 March, limping on back left leg. Tell your supervisor the same day. If an animal is very sick, bleeding badly or down and cannot get up, tell the supervisor at once.

lessons.title: Spotting abnormal behaviour and signs
lessons.html:
Signs that something is wrong

When an animal is sick, hurt or stressed, it often acts differently. Compare what you see with what is normal.

Abnormal signWhat it might mean
Standing alone, head downSick or in pain
Not eating, not chewing the cudSick, sore mouth, stomach problem
LimpingSore foot, injury, foot rot
Fast or hard breathing, coughingLung problem, heat stress
Runny dung, dirty tailWorms, diarrhoea, wrong feed
Swollen belly on the left sideBloat. This is an emergency.
Lying down and cannot get upVery sick, injured or giving birth with problems
Very thinWorms, not enough food, long-term illness
Rubbing, scratching, losing hair or woolLice, mange, ticks, scab

Decide how serious it is

  • Urgent: bloat, heavy bleeding, animal down, trouble giving birth, many sudden deaths. Call the supervisor now.
  • Soon: limping, not eating, coughing. Report today.
  • Watch: a little thin, a few ticks. Note it and look again tomorrow.

Important

Many sudden deaths in a herd can mean a serious disease. Do not touch or cut open a dead animal. Keep other animals away and tell the supervisor at once. Some diseases, like anthrax, can make people very ill.

lessons.title: Moving and restraining animals safely
lessons.html:
Moving animals into a holding facility

A holding facility is a kraal, pen or crush where animals are kept for a short time. Move animals calmly. Stressed animals get hurt and can hurt you.

How animals see and move

  • Animals can see almost all around them, but not straight behind.
  • Every animal has a flight zone. When you step into it, the animal moves away.
  • Animals follow each other. Move them in groups.
  • They do not like dark places, shadows, noise or sudden movement.

Steps

  1. Check the kraal and gates. Close holes in the fence. Open the gate you need.
  2. Walk slowly behind and to the side of the group.
  3. Use a flag, board or your arms. Do not shout.
  4. Let the leaders go in. The rest will follow.
  5. Close the gate behind them.

Restraining animals

Restraint means holding an animal still so it can be checked or treated. Use the right facility:

  • Cattle: move them through the race into the crush. Close the head clamp gently. Close the back bar so the animal cannot move back.
  • Sheep and goats: hold in a small pen. Hold the sheep under the jaw and at the tail end. Never lift by the wool, legs or tail.
  • Pigs: use a pig board to guide them into a small pen.

Never

  • Never hit, kick or twist tails. This is cruelty under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.
  • Never stand behind a cow or horse.
  • Never go into a pen with a bull alone.
  • Never put your arm through the crush bars while an animal is moving.

Key points

  • Know what a healthy animal looks like so you can see problems.
  • Write down the animal's number, the date and what you saw, and report it.
  • Bloat, heavy bleeding and animals that cannot get up are emergencies.
  • Move animals calmly in groups, using the flight zone.
  • Use the crush or a small pen to restrain animals and never hit them.

quiz.question: Which is a sign of a healthy cow?

options.text: It stands alone with its head down
It is alert and chews the cud when resting

quiz.question: What should you write when you see a sick animal?

options.text: The animal's number, the date and what you saw
The name of the farm owner

quiz.question: A cow has a swollen belly on the left side. What is this?
What happens when you step into an animal's flight zone?
How should you hold a sheep?

options.text: Under the jaw and at the tail end, never by the wool

quiz.question: If many animals die suddenly, you should cut one open to see why.
Animals follow each other, so it is best to move them in groups.
